name: Late-cycle leaf aging / senescence context
summary: Cannabis and hemp leaves can lose chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity as foliage ages and flowering advances, with stronger age and canopy-position effects in older or lower leaves; visible yellowing is neither required nor sufficient to classify the change as normal senescence.
affectedParts: whole canopy only as a mapped age gradient
inflorescences and sugar leaves as exclusion-check tissue
stages: flowering time series; Stillwater evidence compares weeks 1, 5, and 9 after transition to a 12-hour photoperiod
vegetative Cherry Wine hemp leaf-aging physiology; not a late-flower symptom sequence
indicators: Change is gradual across serial observations rather than abrupt between captures
Older or lower-position fan leaves change before recently expanded upper-canopy leaves
Chlorophyll index or photosynthetic capacity declines with documented leaf age even when a leaf remains visibly green
The same cultivar and production cohort shows a repeatable late-cycle age and canopy-position gradient
Inflorescences, recently expanded leaves, stems, and roots lack independent evidence of a spreading disorder
Color assessment is made under calibrated or repeatable lighting with healthy same-cultivar references

In controlled flowering Gelato 29, lower fan leaves in the adequately nourished control developed chlorosis in weeks six through eight; this is contextual evidence that yellowing can overlap nutrient deficiency, not a universal normal-fade schedule
exclusions: Visible yellowing alone is used as proof of senescence or harvest readiness
Recently expanded or upper-canopy leaves decline first or as strongly as older lower leaves without an established age gradient
Chlorosis begins early, progresses rapidly, reduces whole-plant vigor, or spreads independently of leaf age
Interveinal chlorosis, marginal scorch, discrete lesions, rings, mosaic, distortion, brittle growth, webbing, feeding scars, frass, or visible organisms are present
Root-zone pH, EC, water content, oxygenation, root appearance, or irrigation history is abnormal
Feed composition, tissue or solution analysis, or response to correction supports nitrogen or another nutrient disorder
Inflorescence mold, necrosis, odor, collapse, or laboratory evidence supports a pathogen
A lamp, spray, heat, cold, drought, salinity, or other exposure gradient explains the distribution better
A yellow leaf is declared a healthy control or negative nutrient-disease sample without linked production and exclusion records
Different leaves or plants are substituted across a supposed progression sequence without persistent specimen identifiers

progression.description: Keep vegetative Cherry Wine leaf-aging measurements separate from flowering Stillwater observations. Neither pooling across studies nor aligning days after full leaf expansion with weeks after photoperiod transition creates a same-plant image or video timeline.
At flowering transition, map leaf node, canopy position, cultivar, photoperiod, PPFD, root-zone measurements, color reference, and a matched healthy plant.

Leaf chlorophyll index and photosynthetic capacity may decline with physiological age. In one Stillwater trial, upper- and lower-canopy chlorophyll indices were lower at weeks 5 and 9 than week 1, while a separate hemp study found declining photosynthetic capacity over 42 days even though leaves stayed green.

Document whether pale green, yellow, anthocyanin-associated red or purple, necrosis, or abscission develops and whether it follows leaf age and canopy position. Published Cannabis evidence does not establish a mandatory color or timing sequence.
Rapid spread, new-growth involvement, lesions, distortion, root abnormalities, pest signs, or inflorescence decline moves the sample out of the normal-development reference class pending diagnosis.

lookAlikes: Nitrogen deficiency or under-supply during flowering
Magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, sulfur, or micronutrient disorder
Water shortage or excessive vapor demand
Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium, or other root disease
Beet curly top virus or unresolved systemic mosaic syndrome
Powdery mildew, Botrytis, or leaf-spot disease
Hemp russet mite, broad mite, spider mite, or thrips injury
High-light, heat, cold, spray, or plant-growth-regulator injury
Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not label “normal fade,” senescence, ripeness, harvest readiness, nutrient depletion, or plant health from color in one photograph or video.
Record leaf node, leaf age, upper versus lower canopy, cultivar, flowering day, photoperiod, PPFD, temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, irrigation, and serial rate of change.
Capture whole-plant, canopy, branch, upper-leaf-surface, lower-leaf-surface, root-zone, and inflorescence views under repeatable lighting with a color reference and scale.

Measure root-zone pH, EC, water content or container weight, and inspect roots; review feed composition and, when consequential, use calibrated solution or tissue analysis rather than assuming remobilization.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification for mites, thrips, webbing, eggs, cast skins, frass, and feeding scars.
Use a plant diagnostic laboratory when lesions, systemic distortion, vascular or root decline, inflorescence disease, or virus/viroid signs remain plausible.
Compare several healthy same-cultivar plants from the same propagation cohort; an age-position gradient that repeats across serial observations is contextual support, not causal proof.

Retain persistent plant and leaf identifiers linking serial node-marked photographs, paired root-zone measurements, feeding records, and any tissue or diagnostic report; keep leaf age separate from calendar flowering day.

Distinguish observed late-cycle color change, supported age-related physiology, and a normal-development reference after competing causes have been excluded; yellow foliage alone is not a negative nutrient or pathogen assay.
immediateActions: Keep the sample labeled “late-cycle leaf aging—cause unresolved” until exclusion checks are complete.
Preserve serial images and measured root-zone, environment, and nutrition records before changing the program.
Isolate or pause propagation from plants with systemic, pest, pathogen, or viroid warning signs.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured nutrient, pH, EC, irrigation, environment, pest, or pathogen problems; do not force yellowing or apply nitrogen solely from camera color.
Reassess recently expanded leaves, roots, and inflorescences after any evidence-based correction while recognizing that old yellow or necrotic tissue will not become a clean health indicator.
Retain the normal-development label only when progression remains slow, age-positioned, cultivar-consistent, and unsupported by competing diagnoses.
prevention: Maintain same-cultivar flowering timelines with leaf-node and canopy-position annotations.
Keep calibrated pH and EC records, irrigation history, environmental logs, pest scouting, and laboratory results linked to image and video samples.
Create healthy reference captures under fixed lighting and camera settings rather than relying on internet photographs or a universal week-of-flower chart.
warnings: A hemp leaf-aging study found photosynthetic capacity could decline while leaves remained green, so visible yellowing is not required for senescence.

The Stillwater flowering study found temporal and canopy-position changes but did not resolve how much was caused by leaf age versus whole-plant ontogeny and did not validate a universal visible fade.
Flowering Cannabis still responds materially to nitrogen and phosphorus supply; withholding nutrients to manufacture a fade is not evidence of normal development.
Color is not a validated harvest-maturity marker and this record does not recommend harvest timing, flushing, or a universal feeding concentration.
The source experiments used limited cultivars and defined production systems; their weeks and nutrient concentrations must not be generalized as thresholds.

The CC BY 4.0 Figure 4 is a vegetative leaf-age physiology diagram, not a normal-fade photograph, healthy-control image, or harvest-maturity standard. Longitudinal Cannabis photographs/video with causal exclusions remain gaps; source wording about CO2 compensation-point direction requires human review.
All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.
The 0.20 image-only ceiling is an annotation safeguard, not a measured diagnostic accuracy estimate.

The Gelato 29 control result came from one cultivar and a small controlled deep-water-culture study; its weeks six through eight do not establish a harvest window, an expected cultivar-independent color sequence, or a reason to withhold nutrients.

sources.title: Cannabis Yield, Potency, and Leaf Photosynthesis Respond Differently to Increasing Light Levels in an Indoor Environment
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Rodriguez-Morrison et al.)
supportedClaims: Indoor-grown Cannabis sativa Stillwater was exposed during flowering to average canopy PPFDs from 120 to 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.
Dry inflorescence yield increased linearly through the highest tested PPFD even though leaf-level photosynthesis saturated below 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.

The high-light experiment did not establish a universal PPFD injury threshold or validate cupping, bleaching, or edge necrosis as light-specific visual symptoms; light exposure must be interpreted with cultivar, acclimation, canopy position, temperature, carbon dioxide, and water status.

In Stillwater during the 12-hour flowering phase, chlorophyll-content index was higher in week 1 than weeks 5 and 9 and was consistently higher in upper- than lower-canopy fan leaves; the authors described evidence of early senescence but stated that the contributions of leaf age and plant ontogeny to diminished week-9 photosynthesis were unresolved.
The study measured chlorophyll index and physiology rather than validating a yellow-leaf appearance, harvest date, or universal late-flower-fade sequence.

sources.title: Leaf Age and Position Effects on Quantum Yield and Photosynthetic Capacity in Hemp Crowns
supportedClaims: Hemp leaves at three crown positions were followed from full expansion for 42 days; photosynthetic capacity declined with leaf age regardless of crown position, light intensity, or photoperiod.
The measured leaves remained green while photosynthetic capacity declined, demonstrating that physiological aging is not equivalent to visible yellowing.

The experiment evaluated aging leaves before abscission in hemp crowns and did not establish a drug-type Cannabis harvest cue, a cultivar-independent color sequence, or proof that visible chlorosis is normal.

The leaf-aging experiment used vegetative Cannabis sativa Cherry Wine; Figure 4e reports leaf spectral index, a greenness/chlorophyll proxy, rather than a photographic yellowing sequence. Its physiological decline must not be relabeled as late-flower symptom progression.

Figure 4 pools three-day leaf-age bins across treatments and crown positions, with means, standard errors, and bubble diameters encoding sample size; the plotted points are not individual plant photographs or a matched symptom timeline.

The Results prose first groups the CO2 compensation point with decreasing parameters, but later describes its increase and Figure 4d plots an increasing curve. This directional inconsistency is retained for human review, not adopted as a diagnostic rule.

sources.title: Optimisation of Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium for Soilless Production of Cannabis sativa in the Flowering Stage Using Response Surface Analysis
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Bevan et al.)
supportedClaims: A high-THC Cannabis cultivar grown in deep-water culture during flowering showed quadratic inflorescence-yield responses to nitrogen and phosphorus, with predicted optima near 194 mg per litre nitrogen and 59 mg per litre phosphorus under the tested conditions.

Inflorescence yield decreased markedly outside approximately 160–230 mg per litre nitrogen and 40–80 mg per litre phosphorus, demonstrating that flowering plants still respond materially to nutrient supply.
Those solution concentrations are experiment- and cultivar-specific and must not be converted into universal feed targets, tissue sufficiency ranges, or visual thresholds.

sources.title: Foliar Symptomology, Nutrient Content, Yield, and Secondary Metabolite Variability of Cannabis Grown Hydroponically with Different Single-Element Nutrient Deficiencies
supportedClaims: Three Gelato 29 plants per treatment were grown in aerated deep-water culture; single-element withholding began with the switch to a 12-hour flowering photoperiod, plants were examined daily and photographed weekly, and upper- and lower-canopy foliage was laboratory analyzed at symptom onset.
Nitrogen-withheld plants showed reduced vegetative expansion before foliar symptoms; during week three, very slight yellowing began at leaflet tips of lower-canopy fan leaves.

By week four, most fan leaves in the lower two-thirds were yellowing; chlorosis was initially strongest between veins before broad whole-leaf yellowing, and severity within leaflets progressed from base toward tip.

By week five, nearly all fan leaves were yellow with severity increasing from bottom to top; petioles became red-brown, some fan leaves browned and senesced, stems began yellowing, and sugar-leaf chlorosis began.

By weeks six and seven, most fan leaves had senesced, older and lower-position sugar leaves progressively yellowed or browned, and stems became brown; the authors considered this prolonged severe endpoint commercially damaging.

At symptom onset, upper- and lower-canopy foliar nitrogen concentrations did not differ and overlapped the control and other treatments, illustrating limitations of a single tissue analysis later in production.

Healthy control plants developed lower-fan-leaf chlorosis in weeks six through eight despite adequate nutrient solution and foliar concentrations, demonstrating that natural late-flower senescence can visually confound nitrogen deficiency.

Figure 1 shows the control at week five without visible foliar deficiency symptoms (a), followed by increasing fan-leaf chlorosis at weeks six (b), seven (c) and eight (d). Results describe oldest main-stem fan leaves first, a bottom-to-top gradient, leaflet-edge-to-midrib spread and greater chlorosis toward smaller radial leaflets; these are one-cultivar observations, not universal normal-fade criteria.

Nitrogen-withheld plants had 73% less aboveground vegetative fresh mass and approximately 72% less fresh inflorescence mass than controls under this three-plant treatment; these are experiment-specific loss estimates, not universal predictions.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage nitrogen-deficiency progression spanning lower-canopy onset, detached fan-leaf severity, canopy distribution, fan-leaf senescence, stem color, and beginning sugar-leaf chlorosis.

In the calcium-withheld treatment, lower fan leaves developed interveinal spots with yellow rings and necrotic brown centers in week three; by week four symptoms occupied mostly the lower two-thirds and were concentrated near leaflet margins and tips.

By week five, spots coalesced into irregular marginal necrosis, serration points browned, injury moved upward into younger fan and sugar leaves, and upper fan-leaf tips curled upward; by week six most fan and sugar leaves were affected.

The flowering-stage lower-leaf onset differed markedly from the vegetative-stage T1 study and from the usual expectation for an immobile nutrient; lower-canopy foliage also contained almost three times the calcium of upper-canopy foliage at symptom onset.

Calcium-withheld plants averaged 621 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls under this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; those values do not establish a universal yield-loss estimate.
Figure 5 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel Cannabis calcium-deficiency progression from week-three spotting through widespread marginal necrosis and upward curling in week six.

Despite foliar iron concentrations less than half those of controls, iron-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants showed no visible deficiency symptoms and no significant aboveground biomass reduction by the end of the 7.5-week treatment.

The symptom-negative flowering result came from three plants in one cultivar and one deep-water-culture experiment; it demonstrates that absence of a visible syndrome cannot exclude inadequate iron status, not that flowering Cannabis never shows iron-deficiency symptoms.

In sulfur-withheld flowering Gelato 29, recently developed upper sugar leaves yellowed in week four; by week five upper fan leaves angled upward and lower fan leaves developed interveinal chlorosis from midrib to margins, later progressing through fan leaves to total yellowing and senescence while early sugar-leaf chlorosis changed little except for browned tips and marginal teeth.

Sulfur-withheld foliage had substantially lower sulfur than all other treatments, with no significant upper-versus-lower canopy concentration difference; inflorescence yield was 34% lower than control while vegetative biomass, root biomass, and cannabinoid concentrations showed no major effect in the three-plant treatment.

Figure 7 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel sulfur-deficiency progression showing younger sugar-leaf yellowing, upward-angled upper fan leaves, a fan-leaf chlorosis sequence, and the later whole-plant distribution.

The flowering study contrasted with the vegetative T1 study in first described canopy location and progression direction, and cautioned that late-flower nutrient symptomology can be confounded with natural foliar senescence.

No visually obvious manganese-deficiency signs developed in the manganese-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants; at week seven their apical inflorescences were similar to controls in size, shape, and color, and the treatment did not reduce biomass or cannabinoid concentrations.

At harvest, manganese-withheld upper-canopy foliage was extremely low in manganese relative to lower-canopy foliage and other treatments, yet the plants remained visually similar to controls, so a symptom-negative image cannot exclude low manganese status.

The authors state that nutrient diagnosis should integrate fertilizer and leachate composition, symptomology, and strategically timed and positioned foliar analysis because cultivar, environment, maturity, and sample location affect tissue concentrations.

Figure 9 is a CC BY 4.0 side-by-side comparison of manganese-withheld and control apical inflorescences during week seven; it is a controlled symptom-negative reference rather than a visible-deficiency example.

Magnesium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for three weeks; mild interveinal chlorosis began on lower fan leaves in week four between the midrib and margins, then rapidly predominated on smaller, younger fan leaves while older fan leaves and inflorescence sugar leaves were less affected.

Severely affected flowering leaves developed interveinal necrosis that increased from leaflet bases toward tips; by week five symptoms were widespread except at apical inflorescences, and by week six most smaller fan leaves and sugar leaves were yellow except at the midrib and extreme margins while some older fan leaves remained largely unaffected.

At symptom onset, lower-canopy foliage in the magnesium-withheld treatment contained about one-third the magnesium of upper-canopy foliage; the treatment averaged 748 g fresh inflorescence mass versus 1110 g in controls, approximately 30% lower in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment, while cannabinoid concentrations were not significantly affected.

Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 five-panel flowering-stage magnesium-deficiency progression spanning the first mild lower-fan-leaf chlorosis, whole-plant distribution, detached-leaf severity, inflorescence context, and advanced whole-plant symptoms.

Potassium-withheld flowering Gelato 29 plants had no visible symptoms for two weeks; in week three, larger sugar leaves developed dark-brown lesions around secondary branch veins, while lower fan leaves developed lighter browning at leaflet tips and marginal teeth one week later.

By week five both potassium-deficiency pathways appeared on the same plant: sugar-leaf lesions predominated near the top and fan-leaf injury was strongest in the middle third, with light-brown fan-leaf injury moving inward especially through interveinal tissue.

By week six, green tissue was largely limited to inflorescences, sugar-leaf midribs, and some lower fan leaves; by week seven most non-inflorescence leaves were brown, curled, and dry, and some inflorescence leaves developed tip browning.

Potassium-withheld plants averaged 535 g fresh inflorescence mass compared with 1110 g in controls and had the second-lowest root dry mass in this three-plant-per-treatment experiment; higher THCA concentration did not offset the lower plant-level yield.
Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 four-panel flowering-stage potassium-deficiency progression showing distinct sugar-leaf and fan-leaf symptoms at week four and their middle-canopy distribution by week five.

useLimitations: Primary full-text XML, figure caption, methods and CC BY 4.0 license inspected through Europe PMC on 2026-10-15; publisher PNG inspected and hashed.
Diagram-only evidence: green bubbles encode sample size, not leaf color, treatment identity, severity, healthy controls, or diagnostic class.
Three-day age-bin means and standard errors pool treatments and crown positions; do not interpret plotted points as independent photographed plants or source groups.
Leaf age is days after full expansion in vegetative hemp, not flowering day or harvest readiness. Leaf spectral index is a measured proxy, not a camera-color or photosynthetic-capacity assay.

Source-text discrepancy: the first Results sentence groups CO2 compensation point with decreases, while later text and panel d indicate an increase; retain human review and do not derive a diagnostic threshold from either wording.

useLimitations: Primary Europe PMC XML license, Figure 1 caption and control Results reviewed on 2026-10-15; publisher PNG visually inspected, hashed and persisted unchanged.
Keep panels a–d mapped to weeks five–eight after flowering transition; these weekly photographs are not continuous video, independent plants, or panel-level severity standards.

The three-plant control treatment and reported adequate nutrient solution/tissue measurements do not supply panel-linked sample identifiers or pathogen-negative assays. Do not infer disease freedom or verified healthy training negatives.

Oldest main-stem fan leaves and later lower-to-upper chlorosis are one-cultivar context. Leaf node, physiological age and persistent photographed-plant identifiers are not supplied; do not invent them.

Whole-plant framing lacks a metric scale and calibrated color reference; later panels emphasize upper canopy. Lighting/background cast and framing prevent calibrated color or same-leaf pixel comparisons.
Do not infer harvest readiness, universal fade timing, fertilizer withholding or nitrogen deficiency from this control composite.
